In other words, broad-based selling pressure has been almost nonexistent so far in 2026.

I talked about @1inch Aqua and the new farming opportunity on my radar not too long ago.

So I'm following up with a practical example of how I'd actually use it.

I started with ~$82 worth of USDC and WETH and created two positions using the same wallet balance.

That gave me roughly $139 in available liquidity, or about 1.7x my original balance in quoted liquidity, without leverage or adding more funds. The only cost was native ETH gas.

You're automatically enrolled (no signup needed), and rewards are based on the trading volume your liquidity actually fills, not the size of your position.

There’s also a pretty big incentive budget behind it: 10M 1INCH in rewards, plus a 500K USDC boost from the 1inch DAO, distributed via Merkl across 80+ markets.

The most interesting part is that my tokens never actually left my wallet. Aqua only uses a revocable approval - the contracts don't custody your funds.

Capital efficiency is one of the biggest LP bottlenecks, and shared liquidity is one answer to that. But I wonder what the fee difference looks like over a full month versus running the same capital in a single pool. Might test that next.

Disclosure: I'm a long-time 1inch user & supporter. Rewards depend on the volume your positions actually fill. My numbers aren't typical or predictive, and rewards aren't guaranteed.

i’m assuming your question is “why does fomo serve US customers while hyperliquid refuses to” and not “how come fomo is able to use apple pay but hyperliquid doesn’t”. those are different questions with different answers

as to the question of serving americans. perpetual swaps of commodities like bitcoin are considered to be under the jurisdiction of the CFTC which has strict rules for how issuers and brokers should operate. hyperliquid structurally cannot comply with those, so american traders are out of the question

memecoins aren’t in the CFTC’s jurisdiction, and the SEC already clarified that they’re not in its jurisdiction either, so they’re just not regulated by anyone. therefore there’s (currently) nothing preventing self-custodial apps like fomo from serving americans

(btw fomo does allow people to trade perps on hyperliquid via the app. it just isn’t available in the US)

tweets.text: Pokemon card market still actively making ATHs, although the focus has branched out into the more obscure stuff which is a similar indicator to altseason in terms of where the cycle is imo. We have also seen a wave of fake goldstars on par with superfake watches, if you are not an expert you are not going to spot them. I am gradually selling into market strength. I think we have to reckon with a double-edged thesis here. Post-scarcity society means significantly greater capital for pastimes & attention share of brand names; Pokemon is the pinnacle of this. But with this comes bad actors empowered by AI and robotics; there is a realistic price cap on the card market where it becomes economically viable to run an industrial scale counterfeiting operation of flawless copies. This is a difficult to quantify tail risk, and I am not saying this is even realistic in the next few years, but I do wonder what the defensive options are here.

I will make $30,000 a month.

I will make $30,000 months normal.

I will stop treating a $30,000 month like it is some distant, impossible number to reach.

I will build the skills, leverage and reputation required to earn it consistently.

I will spend my time on making work that can actually produce $30,000 months.

I will create more value than I consume.

I will charge according to the value I create, not according to what feels comfortable.

I will pursue bigger opportunities.

I will invest in the things that increase my skills, network, distribution and leverage.

I will become comfortable asking for more.

I will become comfortable receiving more.

I will become comfortable being responsible for more.

I will take the actions today that the $30,000-a-month version of me would take without hesitation.

I will remember that he did not become that person earning $30,000 a month overnight.

He built himself through thousands of decisions made in the right direction.

Every day I operate like him, I close the gap.

$30,000 a month will eventually stop feeling like a goal.

It will become my new normal.

Quick observation on why AI has exploded at work, but has been slow to disrupt consumer apps:

At work, AI follows patterns and gets rid of drudgery (good!)

At home, AI follows patterns but it generates slop (bad!)

This is why AI has taken off at work, but not so much for consumer apps and experiences (social, entertainment, dating, etc)

Much of work is drudgery - filling out forms, following processes, writing updates, reviewing boilerplate code, etc. - and AI does a great job compressing this down the boring steps so that humans can focus on the high-leverage steps. The boring/routine work is not hard, but they often take a lot of steps and you have to stitch together a lot of data. You follow patterns. AI is good at following patterns too.

Consumer attention, on the other hand, is hard to win over because people crave novelty, seek parasocial relationships, and are so cognizant of AI slop. A video of an attractive person talking loses its ability to generate parasocial relationships. In domains like social media, video, etc where authenticity is paramount, a distorted AI sign in the background can ruin the entire thing. Novelty is generated by surfing the cultural wave with something new and unique - AI slop often pattern matches to the past, after all, it’s the past that’s in the data set, and as a result, new/unique is hard

This is a form of “adversarial creativity” - and it exists in business as well. When you think about inherently adversarial activities in business - like sales and marketing, where novel messaging, competitive move+countermove dominate - AI has received the most scrutiny for generating slop. No one wants the same sounding AI generated cold emails. No one wants to use AI slop software. You have to go outside the model in order to really land a message.

Perhaps this is the ultimate human-in-the-loop problem, because to do something fresh and unique requires adversarial creativity. Or maybe with enough advancements around being able to observe and react in real-time, future AI models will be able to say something novel by taking into account the X timeline from the past 24 hours.

One clarification on the $24.7M/MW, since some might read it as an annual number. It is not.

The $105B is a lifetime cap on the whole deal. Divided by 4,250 MW, that is the most NVIDIA could ever pay per megawatt, total.

How the payment works: The Agreements specify a guaranteed minimum value (undisclosed so far) for each lease. If OpenAI defaults or goes insolvent, SB Energy re-lets or sells the space, and NVIDIA pays the shortfall between that guaranteed minimum and what the re-let or sale brings in.

What we do not know is what sets the guaranteed minimum. It could either be the rent remaining on the lease, or what the building cost to construct. A rent-based promise shrinks as OpenAI pays. A cost-based one may not shrink at all.

Testing the rent case: NVIDIA stands behind this lease, so it should discount closer to an investment-grade cost of capital than to an equity rate. At 6-8%, the NOI Portsmouth needs to justify a $24.7M/MW promise over 20 years is $2.15-2.52M/MW/year.

RIOT's Rockdale lease is the most recent public comp. 191 MW, 20 years, $9.1B of contract revenue and $365-411M average annual NOI per the company, or roughly $2.0M/MW/year. Portsmouth would need to price 8-25% above that for the remaining rent to equal $24.7M/MW at the start of the lease. Seems entirely plausible for greenfield with a 20-year term. So the rent case holds up.

The cost case also fits. $24.7M/MW lines up with the $25-31M/MW it takes to build the non-silicon half of a greenfield campus.

The Agreement will get filed with NVIDIA's 10-Q later this month and settle the logic.

Open to other interpretations. Any ideas?

Lukas, is the purpose of life to become rich, or to become wiser, happier?

Usually when I meet people who got rich very quickly from Bitcoin or some one trick wonder, I notice something missing. They have money, but often they’re still confused, jumping from one experience to another because they can afford it: yachts, parties, drugs, women, whatever comes next.

And if you don’t know who I’m talking about, just go to Ibiza in the summer. You’ll meet plenty of them. Rich people getting drunk, getting high, jumping from one yacht to another, one party to another, one model to another, constantly looking for the next experience.

When you make money slowly, through struggle, something very different happens. You make mistakes. You learn. You calibrate. You learn to deal with fear, greed, ego, uncertainty, failure. You get knocked down and learn how to get back up. And those lessons don’t only make you a better investor. They make you stronger and better equipped to deal with problems everywhere else in life.

The struggle also teaches appreciation. A person who climbed the mountain will appreciate the view very differently from someone who arrived at the top in a helicopter.

The money is not the most valuable thing you gain. It’s the person you had to become to earn it.

I've been trying this for half a year, and the returns are decent (vastly better than DeFi stablecoin farming), but not linear enough to be certain about consistency

One problem is that to optimize the PnL curve of the account, you have to spend more time on it, which sort of defeats the purpose of it being a 'passive investment'

The most important thing to do is to be super conservative about sizing, because one wrong trade with too much relative size can completely fuck your gains, which are accumulated slowly through small wins

There's also a risk of tilting at some point, ie of not respecting your strict risk management rules (required to have very limited drawdowns), which can quickly erase weeks/months of returns too

Overall I'm quite happy about the strategy anyway, but I think I should run it with more size + spend more time on it, so that it becomes a conservative subaccount with material gains rather than a passive account with small size
